inline.s: He also said: It is not only resentment and anger that must not be left to settle overnight. Even the wish to have parents and brothers act according to heavenly principle, and to have parents and brothers love and cherish us — though this be a kindly intent — must not be too eager in the heart, nor handled too heavily. For if it is too heavy, it takes hold and will not turn.

He also said: There are four kinds of parents whose need for filial care is most urgent, and toward whom the sin of unfilial conduct is graver than toward others. The first is the aged; the second, the sick; the third, the widowed and bereaved; the fourth, the poor and destitute. When parents were in their prime they could still manage their own eating, rest, and daily movements. But when they are frail and stooped, leaning on a staff and easily toppling, passing cold, lonely nights when their iron bones are hard to bear; or again when a lingering illness keeps them ever ill at ease, their waste and filth gathered in a heap, their mats and bedding repulsive — it is at such a time that the son finds it hardest to serve, and at such a time that the parents most depend upon the son. So too, when in old age they have lost their spouse — who asks whether they are warm or cold? Shadow and form face each other, and the heart's words go unspoken. A husband can still bear it; a widowed mother — what is she to do? Though sons and grandsons fill the hall, the coupled are coupled and the young are young; each sleeps soundly and returns to his own joy. The long watches of the night are hard to bear; beside the pillow tears fall in secret with no one to tell. If there are filial sons and grandsons able to tend them, a little of their coldness may still be entrusted to a warm heart. But when the mother who bore me has grown used to willfulness and the mother-in-law bars the way with a cold face, nursing only the little blood that remains and gaining only a lifetime of misery — again, when there is not enough to raise the children and the wedding costs drain all strength, while the hale young grow sleek and warm and the old and poor scratch their heads in perplexity, gazing at one delicacy with watering mouth, swallowing indignation to beg a few meals, cooking at night and at dawn and still cursed for eating at leisure, spinning and holding grandchildren and still cursed for being slow to die — this several kinds of parents have a resentment enough to move Heaven. For their descendants, filial conduct should be all the greater, beyond that of ordinary children; and those who exhort and guide others should be all the more urgent here.

Chen Chengqing, in the Complete Book of Exhortation and Admonition, adds another class, saying: There are those who are bondmaids and concubines yet are the natural mothers of children. They are likewise women, born in poor and lowly homes and fallen into the hands of the rich and honored. The nights of sharing the same quilt are few, the nights of lying alone and sleeping solitary are many. Those with good fortune may meet a virtuous, kind mistress, and with half sunshine and half rain may barely pass the days. But should they encounter a jealous, fierce temper, all day long harsh words are heaped on them, with every kind of insult. Let them speak a single word in reply and they are charged with overstepping their place and lacking manners; let them make half a plea and they are resented for whispering sedition by the pillow. Then they meet, too, an unfilial daughter-in-law or unfilial children, who, not thinking to pity them for the grandfather's and father's sake, do nothing but stir up trouble against the mother; the servants below take up the refrain. Storms rise from level ground, thunderbolts fall from a clear sky. And it is their misfortune, too, that the master's affection is thin — he knows not their warmth or cold, pities not their pain or illness; within the women's quarters their tears soak the robes, while beyond the door there is joy and feasting. Some dote on a new favorite and cast off the old affection; the ill-fated pity themselves and several times seek death — truly deplorable and heartrending. If by chance they conceive, they go to great lengths to conceal it; when concealment is no longer possible they endure every shame and anger. When the time of childbirth comes, who is there to look after them? If they are fortunate enough to bear a son, jealousy will not permit it; they must be doubly guarded, and it is forever said that, relying on their child, they grow insolent. Should the child fall ill, they carve out their own flesh to cure the sore, gladly suffering cold and hunger. The scripture says: Ten months the mother carries the child in her womb in hardship; three years she nurses and holds him with a diligent heart. If she is a bondmaid and concubine, her toil is ten times the ordinary. When the child grows to manhood and enjoys a wife and children, enjoys fields and houses, he never thinks that all he enjoys today comes from his mother's wasted blood and thin bones, her dried tears and broken heart. When he reflects on this, can he not feel a pang in the nose? A son should ever bear this in mind, rouse and resolve, vowing one day to win renown so as to repay the thousand pains and ten thousand hardships. In his constant service he should remember his mother's toil, that a candle before the wind is a thing to fear, and attend to her early. If he does not give his whole heart and strength, he is more gravely a traitor to filial devotion than an ordinary unfilial son, and will surely soon receive Heaven's punishment.

Where is filial piety fulfilled? Timeliness is the most precious thing. Let it never be that the parents' years grow short while we regret that our hearts were not wholly given; let it never be that our children's strength grows daily greater while we wound ourselves that our parents could not share it. Parents await their sons' support in the years around fifty or sixty. It is like holding a short candle while walking a long road — hurrying toward the inn, we fear we shall not arrive in time; how much less dare we loiter along the way! A son who clasps his wife and children, eats his fill and sleeps in peace — does he not know that the white-haired, dim-eyed old man above the hall has again had one day cut away? His wife's and children's years are still young, and the days they may enjoy are long; but the father and mother who gave him birth have the setting sun already at hand, and the flowing stream gives no pause. Should the least misstep occur, the merest drop of gratitude cannot be repaid — above, below, in heaven and on earth, there is no place to seek them, and he can only sigh at the wind in the trees and shed tears over the fowl and pigs, bequeathing to himself a lifelong and eternal regret. Therefore, let a son each day think on his parents, on the boundless depth of their grace, and on how he cannot always keep them. Then the filial heart will naturally be stirred. There was one who, mourning the dead, said: This frail, unloving body is made of inch by inch of a loving mother's blood; the crow in its tenderness knows no measure, yet a hundred years leave only empty tears. Alas, that such words should be spoken. If we are still spared this, we should practice filial duty at once.
Sima Guang of the Song dynasty said: In serving my parents I did nothing surpassing other men — I was only able not to deceive them. In serving my lord, it was the same.

The great outline of filial piety has four parts: to establish virtue, to carry on the family, to preserve the body, and to nourish the will. In these, circumstances differ and abilities vary, but the point is to accord with one's lot and one's strength, doing all that ought to be done, with a genuine and sincere intent running throughout, to the last closing of the eyes on the deathbed, without a hair's breadth of regret. In such a one, filial piety may be said to be nearly complete.

Mr. Luo said: The filial son, in serving his parents, must not cause them a cold and indifferent heart, must not cause them an anxious heart, must not cause them a fearful heart, must not cause them a sorrowful heart, must not cause them a heart too ashamed to speak, must not cause them a heart of shame and regret.

Yu Tieqiao said: A son must wholly enter into and understand the heart of his parents as they look to their son. The fame and gain of the world are not something to be surely obtained; yet he who studies buries himself in his books, he who farms toils with all his might, he who trades runs his business with all his heart — placing himself in a position where he can be rich and honorable, so that in his parents' mind there may always dwell the fond fancy of becoming the honored master or the wealthy landlord. This too is one knack for nourishing the will. But if a son leaves his parents with no fancy they may harbor, then their hearts are pained indeed.

Wen Jiexiao said: When there is a white-haired elder in the hall, it is the blessing of the descendants. First, old ties are kept in touch; second, the neighbors and fellow villagers are persuaded; third, the sons and grandsons receive their commands and the servants follow the rules; fourth, he speaks of the old stories of ancestors and the models of the district's former worthies; fifth, he settles the violent impatience of the young; sixth, he looks after small and trivial matters.
Wang Zhongshu's Essay on Exhorting Filial Piety says:
In this world there are unfilial sons who idle their floating lives away in vain.
They never think of their parents' grace — how are they different from withered wood?
Before the hundred bones were formed into a man, they lay ten months in the mother's womb.
Thirsty, they drank the mother's blood; hungry, they ate the mother's flesh.
When the child's body was about to be born, the mother's belly was as a place of slaughter.
The father grieved and sorrowed for the mother; the wife wept to her husband.
They dreaded only that at the hour of birth the body would become a companion of ghosts.
The moment they saw the child's face, a life was joyfully renewed.
From then on the loving mother's heart, day and night, diligently nurses and cradles him.
The mother lies on the damp mat, while the child sleeps on a dry, soft quilt.
When the child sleeps soundly, the mother dares not move or stretch.
She hides herself amid the filth and stench, with no time to think of bathing.
Her hairpin awry and her cap askew, she heeds not how she looks.
Each step she dreads a pit or well; each lift of the foot she fears a topple.
She nurses him for three full years — her sweat and blood, how many pints?
Through a thousand hardships and ten thousand bitter pains, until the child is fifteen or sixteen.
His spirit and temper grow gradually headstrong; his actions are hard to restrain.
He roams and revols abroad with friends, giving himself over to wine and lust.
He comes not home by day's end, and she leans at the gate from dusk till dawn.
The child travels a journey of a thousand li; the mother's heart follows a thousand li.
Once he takes a fine wife, their love is as fish and water, all harmony.
He looks on his mother's face as on earth; he looks on his wife's face as on jade.
If the mother reproaches him with one word, he conceals his wrath and glares with both eyes.
If the wife scolds him in a hundred ways, he smiles and answers, not counting it a shame.
The mother wears an old torn skirt; the wife is dressed in new, fine silk.
He does not avoid the loathing of others; he does not understand shame or disgust.
If his parents are widowed and alone, they keep the long nights in solitude.
When well, they are given but one meal; when ill, but one bowl of gruel.
They are left in an empty room, like a traveller passing a single night.
Hastening to become ghosts below the springs, their life like a candle before the wind.
Listless, they come to death, and lone souls are buried in the hill valleys.
Their spirits lie in the dark underworld — who remembers that they are in fetters?
Scarcely have the parents died when the brothers divide the wealth and fortune.
They do not know the grace of their two parents, and speak only of their own good fortune.
All say of such people that they are worse than the beasts and the herds.
The loving crow can feed back to the nest; the lamb still kneels to take the milk.
I exhort you who are a son to be diligent in reading the classics and the books.
Huang Xiang fanned his pillow in summer and warmed the quilt in winter.
Wang Xiang lay on the freezing ice; Meng Zong wept over the withered bamboos.
Guo Ju was willing to bury his child; Ding Lan once carved his parents in wood.
How is it that the people of today do not learn the customs of old?
Do not, with an unfilial head, vainly wear a roof in the world of men.
Do not, with an unfilial body, vainly put on the clothes of men.
Do not, with an unfilial mouth, vainly eat the five grains of men.
Wide as heaven and earth may be, they cannot contain the race of the rebellious.
Repent your former faults quickly, and do not wait for Heaven's punishment.

Mr. Tang's Song of the Parents' Grace says: Before I speak, my tears stream down; hard is it to repay the grace of father and mother's raising me. Of itself this breaks the heart, so that I cannot speak of it — yet I will speak my breaking heart to all. Only the mother, in the pangs of pregnancy, endures torments, and a hundred kinds of demon-tribulation pass her hard to bear. Say not that giving birth has no danger or good fortune; life and death hang on a moment, what is there to do? Now the belly aches so poignantly that she bids someone cut her clothes; a thousand deaths and ten thousand births are hard to count, and she relies only on Heaven and the gods to decide. When the child is born, the blood surges to the heart; her jaws are clenched tight and her eyes roll up. Only after the afterbirth is cut and past the third day does the child count as human. Time and again, urine and excrement spread all over her body — rank, putrid, and foul beyond bearing — yet she has not the least jot of loathing; she washes and changes him over and over with the utmost heartache and toil. Hearing a cry from the child, she turns over and reaches out her hands to hold him. Think, in that first year and a half, what sleep could she ever get? Among the heavy snow of the twelfth month's bitter cold, she nestles her head and face against the child. It is only because the breast is the child's milk that all night she keeps her chest bare to the cold. Hearing that the child has broken out in smallpox, at once she is startled, her eyes rolling up in fear. From the moment the spots appear, all day she has not a drop of rice gruel. She knocks her head and lights a stick of incense, crying again and again upon the Goddess of Pox. If only the goddess would answer her cry, what fear that the child's head be broken and the brain flow out? Happily the child reaches the age of two, and can walk by the table and the stool. She frets only that he will fall and break his head or face; she hangs her heart and clings in concern, never at ease. If the child is born with a crooked temper, she lets his nature run as it will. How is it that the parents are still partial in their love, and still say, 'Good child, how good he is!' Now the child's hair reaches his shoulders, and in the blink of an eye he stands before them grown to manhood. The dear parent's heart is torn and cannot let him go; he can no longer stay forever at her knee. Though he has earned a little farmland, he has borne ten thousand fears and pains — not for his children, not for his daughters? And what, indeed, has he eaten himself, but a few coppers' worth? The mother looks at the father, the father looks at the mother — why is their face all sallow and yellow all day long? It is only because the sons and daughters are to be married, and they sit face to face with furrowed brows in a single room. Inch by inch, thread by thread, all is grace; who can paint even half a hair's breadth of the truth? Even if the Liao E could be depicted, it would only be a six- or seven-tenths likeness.

The Song of Filial Obedience says: When the mother was with child ten months, she trod high and low in fear of harming the child. Do you, the son, keep this meaning in your heart for your whole life; then to correct yourself and honor your parents both will lack nothing. When the doctor's child is feverish or ailing from the cold, she regrets she cannot gouge out her heart and pull out his lungs and liver. If his parents are ever in distress, he should also devise a hundred schemes to win them joy. When anger comes it can frighten the ghosts and startle the gods, yet at the sight of the child the face blossoms into spring. A son, too, should be forever like this — toward his parents never bring the least trace of anger. He holds the child and teaches him to speak and learn his sounds; to laugh and scold at father and mother is a joy to them. When, in days to come, the child comes before the hall to hear instruction, even if scolded and caned, let him not moan. Father and mother and child should not live apart; look upon the blood-drop script of the penal court. There is, moreover, that which cannot be borne to part: the one shriek that breaks open at the first exit from the womb. Brothers were originally of one root; Heaven gave them branches and leaves to be raised up in mutual support. If one thinks of splitting and dividing the household, that is to push away the parents' grace. Riches and honor, poverty and lowliness lie in this body; kings and marquises, slaves and servants are not bound to it. I counsel you, when poor, not to call out in resentment against your parents, and when rich, not to forget the ones who gave you life. Filial duty often is displaced by the love of husband and wife; I counsel you to acknowledge clearly the two parents alone. If a husband dies or a wife dies, they may marry again and remarry; but once parents are gone, can they be reborn? Parents are like the same tree; how can one escape the autumn wind? I counsel you to support them diligently while they live; the weeping after death is always in vain. The body of seven spans stands in this world, yet through the endless heaven it is hard to repay the grace of the two. I counsel you to keep the burial and the offerings at the proper seasons, and often go to the mound to sweep the grave gate.

Jin Shaosong said: As for the ruin of the mourning rites, it has reached its extreme in our day. Everything departs from the ancients, and the practice of taking a wife during the seventh-period mourning is especially without precedent. The gentleman of old, during mourning, found no flavor in sweet food, no pleasure in music, no ease in his dwelling — and this for three years. Yet the heartless, wrong-doing people of today will instead seek a marriage during the seventh-month mourning. They exchange the mat of straw for the bamboo couch, change the coarse mourning hemp for embroidered brocade, set aside the mourning for their parents to seek the joy of husband and wife. Is this in accord with ritual? Is this at peace with the heart? For a son to do this is to be called greatly unfilial; for parents to command their son to do this is to teach him to be greatly unfilial. Further, to carry out a joyous matter amid misfortune — that husband and wife are both inauspicious. Who first set the precedent, I know not, but today it has become the customary fashion. Even among families of ritual and poetry there may be such things; truly such persons are sinners against Zhou and Confucius and should be utterly cut off.

Shen Longjiang said: In a son's serving his parents, nothing is greater than the matter of seeing them to their end. If in this the heart is not completely given, then there is no longer any chance to give it completely. What is to be done when brothers are many and put the blame on one another, and the matter is finished in haste, leaving regrets for later days? I think that the eldest son, if he is able to handle it alone, should take it upon himself without assigning it to the other sons; and of the other sons, whichever can bear it should also make it his own duty, without unfairly burdening the eldest son. Let each devote his whole heart and strive to be first in the effort, and only then are they sons. If a man's heart leans upon another even a tenth part, then in his own heart there is a tenth part he cannot give.

In antiquity mourning made its master sorrow; but the people of today are not sorrowful. In antiquity the sacrifice made its master reverence; but the people of today are not reverent. Both are against ritual, and of the three, the loss of proper rite in burial is the gravest. For this reason I dwell on it with a deep intent. Zhu Zaian said: A high officer waits three months, a common gentleman passes beyond a month; hence if the burial does not take place, they do not change their garments or their fare, mourning the parents who have not yet found their rest. The people of today are deluded by the doctrine of wind and water, and there are those who covet an auspicious site and put things off for a long time; and those who, having buried, are full of doubt and open the grave again and again. They do not think on the meaning of the ancients in choosing a plot — it was only that filial sons and kind grandsons, holding their parents' remains in reverence, keep them from water and wind, from insects and ants, from the plough and the harrow, and in days to come from roads and city walls and ditches. This being sufficient, what more is needed? Was it ever for the parents' bones to be made the instrument of descendants' fortune? Then wind and water need not be coveted. Again, there are those deluded by the doctrine of the separate households; the brothers' discussions are many and hold the matter back through the whole year. Having already chosen the year, month, day and hour, they again doubt the bias of the mountains and waters — as if a father's and mother's having one son the more should only add a day more of their lying exposed. Do they not know that a man's fortune and misfortune each have their own causes and conditions, and what have mountains and waters to do with it? Then the separate-household doctrine need not be clung to. If a man is stubborn and will not awaken, and once he is dragged by gain and fame, he lingers in another land year after year, with almost no hope of a settled home; or he meets fire and water and there is the fear of burning and drowning. Can a son be at ease in his heart? As for the matter of the temporary burial, it must not be long drawn out; if it is long, the rain seeps in, the sun's heat steals upward, and before it returns to the earth the wood is already rotten. The humane man and filial son should also take this deeply to heart.

The filial ones of old — such as Zengzi studying the rites till his lap was wet with tears, Minzi calming his mother with one word, Laolai playing the child and making sport to please his parents, Hua Bao never wearing the cap in grief for his father, Boyu receiving the staff and weeping in sorrow, Wang Pou clasping the cypress and wailing in grief, Guo Ping hiring himself out for labor in order to bury his parents, Jiang Ge working as a hired servant to feed his mother — each possessed a perfect nature and a perfect feeling, standing forth as a model for a hundred generations. Now let me again set out several instances, to tell the people of the world, so that all may together know the pattern.

The Book of Transformation says: The Lord of the Star of Literature, at the beginning of the Zhou dynasty, was born at the meeting of Wu and Kuaiji, and served his parents with perfect filial devotion. His mother was sixty when a boil broke out upon her back. The Lord sucked the boil for three days, when suddenly his mouth was filled; he spat it out and looked — there was a membrane like silk, and pus like milk, and it was the root of the boil. The mother then recovered. But because she had been ill and was long weakened, the physician said: This is a deep-rooted disease; only man's substance can replenish man, and true replenish the true, and then perhaps it may be restored. Whereupon the Lord, in the middle of the night, cut flesh from his thigh, cooked it and presented it to her. Suddenly a voice in the sky said: Heaven, for your pure filial devotion, grants your mother twelve more years. And indeed she recovered. When the Lord was thirty-six, his parents died. He himself took up the basket and spade to make the grave, pillowing his head on the clod beside the mound. At the end of three years, a great flood suddenly broke forth. The Lord fasted and kept vigil beside the grave, reciting the Great Cave Scripture day and night without ceasing, and reverently tending the golden image of the Primordial Beginning, praying to be spared the flood. When the water receded, it was found that the valley before the grave had been turned into a high mound a full li across. From then on, the pines and catalpas were never harmed again. After his death, the Lord of Heaven commanded him to be lord of Mount Jun. Later he was reborn in the Zhang family, and served King Xuan as friend of Yin Jifu — this is the 'Zhang Zhong, filial and friendly' of the Book of Songs. Now the scholars of today worship the Star of Literature daily, yet do not know that he attained the holy fruit entirely through filial devotion and brotherly love. Therefore I record him first, to show the gentleman who studies this.

In the Song dynasty, Zhao Juxian's parents were over ninety and of a stern and hasty nature. Juxian and his wife served them diligently and respectfully, and their filial conduct carried all into harmony. Each day they burned incense, praying for their parents' health and comfort, and pleased them by a hundred contrivances until the close of their days. The Lord of Heaven saw their heart to be single and their will one, and gave to their seven sons and three sons-in-law all unusual degrees. Juxian and his wife together attained the fruit of the immortals.

Yang Fu of Taihe took leave of his parents and went into the land of Shu, seeking the great holy one Wuji. On the road he met an old monk, who asked him whither he was going. He said: I am going to visit Wuji. The monk said: It would be better for you to see the Buddha. He asked: Where is he? The monk said: Only return home, and whoever you see rushing out with slippers on the wrong feet and dressed in a certain color of clothes — that is he. So he turned back. At dusk he knocked at the door. His mother, overjoyed, threw on her clothes and came out with her slippers reversed — she was the Buddha's appearance of which the monk had spoken. Fu was startled to understand. From then on he devoted his whole strength to his parents, and wrote out in his own hand a commentary on the Classic of Filial Piety of several tens of thousands of words. When the inkstone was almost dry, the water suddenly filled the pool — men said it was the response to his filial devotion. The Buddha Maitreya said: There are two Bodhisattvas in the hall, and I grieve that the people of the world do not know them. They are not made of painted gold and silk, nor carved of sandalwood; the living father and mother of the present moment — they are Shakyamuni and Maitreya. If you can revere and serve them to the full, what need to seek merit elsewhere? Mao Qizong said: The eminent men and famous scholars of the Six Dynasties honored the Classic of Filial Piety — some buried it with the dead, some offered it for the spirit. The sick recited it and were healed; those in strife recited it and were reconciled; in fire, they recited it and it ceased — so inconceivable was its power. Therefore Huang Kan recited the Classic of Filial Piety twenty times a day likening it to the Guanyin Sutra. Alas! To abandon the present Buddha and beg the aid of a past Buddha is to be false to one's heart. To not recite the Classic of Filial Piety but seek happy fortune from all the other scriptures — the spirits detest that.

The Treasured Treasury Sutra says: If you serve your parents with filial devotion, the Heavenly Emperor Indra is in your household. If you nourish your parents with filial devotion, the great Brahma Lord is in your household. If you revere your parents with filial devotion, Shakyamuni Buddha is in your household. Thus the bodhisattva Shama gouged out his eyes to save his parents, and his deep affliction was cured in a single morning; the child of compassion made a vow to take on the suffering, and the wheel of fire vanished in an instant. When the utmost sincerity moves Heaven, and true devotion moves the Buddha — from ancient times it has been so, and men should believe it firmly. Now he who follows the Buddha's teaching: he himself observes the precepts, undergoes austere practice, and is also able to lead his parents to fast and chant the Buddha's name — only then does he accord with the Buddha's meaning, and the nine generations of ancestors enter heaven. And so it is for the one who returns to the Way. The vulgar monks and vulgar Taoists of today cannot do this, yet say at once, 'I have left the world to save my parents' — this is but self-deception.

Cui Mian had a most filial nature. His mother lost her sight. He spent the whole family fortune seeking a cure, and for thirty years did not take off his cap and belt in serving her. Whenever there was a beautiful scene or a lucky day, he would be sure to support her and make her laugh, so that the mother forgot her pain. When his mother died, he wasted himself and coughed blood, taking only vegetarian food for the rest of his life. He loved his elder brothers and sisters as he did his mother, and was kinder to his nephews and grandchildren than to his own sons. Of the salary he received he shared it all out, saying: The wind and the trees have already grieved me, and there is no way to spread my filial piety. I think only of those whom my parents held dear — these four or five. Let me treat them all generously, so that in the nine springs my parents may be comforted. Later he rose to be Vice-Minister of the Chancellery. His son, Youfu, was a worthy minister. Ah, Lord Cui was truly a filial son. While they lived he gave them every joy; when they died, he nourished their will. There are those in the world who dwell in wealth and honor yet treat their own brothers and sisters as passers-by, and their maternal uncles and aunts as idle guests. Reading this, can they fail to break into a sweat of shame and reform?

Lü Sheng lost his mother young, and served his father, a man of a hundred years, with perfect filial devotion. As the years advanced, the father could not control his urine and waste. Sheng slept with his father, attending him with all care and obedience, rising four or five times each night. When the soldiers' fire came, he carried his father into the mountains. The bandits were moved by his filial piety and spared them. His father was fond of fine apricots, which a neighbor seized. Sheng wrote an appeal to the god, and the god at once sent a boil upon the back of the wealthy neighbor, telling him to return the apricot land to the filial son, and only then did it cease. Again, Guo Cong lost his father and only his mother remained. He ever harbored the sigh of the boundless grace, and for thirty years ate no meat or wine, praying devoutly morning and evening. His mother lived to one hundred four, with eyes and ears undimmed, and her eating and drinking grew even stronger.

Yang Yi begged for food to support his parents. When he got food, though extremely hungry, he dared not taste it, but offered it first to his parents. When he obtained something sweet, he knelt and presented it, then leapt and danced, singing mountain songs to please them. So he did for ten years. The villagers were moved by his filial piety and gave him money, hiring him as a servant. He would not accept, saying: How can my parents be parted from me for a single day? When both died, he begged for a coffin, and took off his own clothes to wrap them, so that though the cold was severe, he went unclothed without thought for himself. He buried them in the wild, and slept in the open beside the coffin, wailing day and night. At the times of the year he bowed and offered, never failing.

In the Tang dynasty, Li Jiongxiu had a most filial nature. His mother had been of low birth. His wife once scolded a servant-girl, and the mother was displeased and angered. He at once put his wife away. Some asked him why; he said: I took a wife only that she might serve my mother. If she crosses her countenance, how can she be kept? His filial heart reached to Heaven; a mushroom grew in his hall, and Emperor Zhongzong honored his gate.

Gu Xiong was poor and kept a school. Each year his whole income he gave to his father. The father was given to waste. The school-master pitied his poverty and sent him a whole year's stipend at once, saying: Your good father does not know; you could buy land for the autumn harvest. Xiong said: Could I bear to barter my daily filial heart for a few piculs of rice? And he presented it all to his father. When a son, Jiming, was born, he passed the examinations while still young.

Li Qiong took a wife and had a son, then moved into his mother's room. At night he often rose ten times or more. His mother said: You have grown rather frail in recent years; you should seek a maidservant to attend me. Qiong said: Whatever my mother desires, if I do not handle it with my own hands, I feel I have failed. His mother then did not press him, so no servant in the household dared to be idle or lazy.

In the Han dynasty, Cao E of Shangyu had a father, Xu, who was a shaman. On the fifth day of the fifth month, he was welcoming the god upon the river when he fell into the water and drowned. E was fourteen. She sought her father's corpse and could not find it. Along the river she wailed and wept for seven days and nights, then leapt into the river. After five days she came up bearing her father's corpse on the surface. The magistrate of Shangyu, Du Shang, reported the matter and memorialized that she be honored as a filial daughter. A shrine was built by the river, where to this day she is worshipped.

In the Song dynasty, the filial woman Wu lost her husband early and had no son. She served her mother-in-law with perfect filial devotion. The mother-in-law was old and blind, and, thinking of Wu's loneliness, wished to adopt a son. Wu wept and said: A chaste woman does not serve a second husband. I will strive to wait upon her with all my strength. Wu spun hemp and reeled silk for the village, and with the money she got she supported her mother-in-law. When she got fine food she would necessarily hide it in her breast to bring home. One day when the rice was not yet cooked, the neighbor's mother called her out. The mother-in-law thought the rice was overdone, and was about to take it into a basin; but because she could not see, she spilled it by mistake into the waste bucket. When Wu returned, she did not ask, but hurried to the neighbor's to borrow cooked rice for her mother-in-law. She drew water, washed the spoiled rice several times, steamed it, and ate it herself. One day she dreamed that two blue-robed lads came riding on the clouds, bearing a written summons, saying the Heavenly Emperor had called her. They led her into audience, and the Emperor said: You are but a village woman, yet you can serve your old mother-in-law with diligence and whole-hearted toil — this is truly worthy of honor. I grant you a thousand cash, so that you may return and serve her meals; from now on you need not work. Then he ordered the two lads to escort her back. She saw that at the head of the bed there were indeed a thousand cash. When these were used up, another thousand appeared, never coming to an end.

Qiu Duo buried his mother on the plain of Mount Fengming, weeping and crying: While Duo lived, he never left his mother's side by a hair's breadth. Now she is gone — can I abandon this body and soul in a waste where no one comes? He built a hut beside the grave, and at morning and evening offered food as if she were alive. On dark nights of cold and when the bleak wind moaned, Duo feared his mother was lonely, so he would pace the grave wailing and crying: Duo is here. The place was full of tigers; but hearing Duo's weeping, they shrank away. Men called him a true filial son.

In the Ming dynasty, Wu Zhang lost his father young. At ten years of age his mother, née Lu, in the Yongle period, was selected by the rule and entered the palace, and followed the prince to his fief at Shaozhou in Guangdong. When Zhang heard of it he was so moved that tears streamed down. He abandoned his home to seek his mother. In the boat he set up an image of Guanyin and bowed to it in worship, praying that he might see his mother. His sincerity was earnest, and his weeping was most piteous. On the road he fell ill with dysentery, rising a hundred times a day and night; and even in his delirium he kept calling 'mother' without ceasing. When he reached Shaozhou, his mother had already been transferred with the prince to the new fief at Jiangxi. He went by land to Raozhou, rushing over the sandy wastes till both his feet were swollen and he lay in the wild. A Taoist, who called himself Jiao, came and took medicine and applied it, and he was healed at once. Crossing a mountain pass he met a black snake that bit his foot, and he fell to the ground. Again he saw the Taoist Jiao arrive, who applied medicine, and the pain stopped. He lodged in a lonely village, and before dawn set out. He met a great snow and rested in an old temple. Again he saw the Taoist Jiao come, who patted him and said: To risk your body like this for your mother — a true iron man indeed. He brought out a cake and gave it to him, and at once he forgot hunger and cold. Arriving at Raozhou, he learned his mother was at the prince's residence. He submitted a petition to see her; it was not granted. So he rented a room in the residence, and wrote in large characters 'Longing for my parents', and pasted up beside it: 'Seeking my kin across ten thousand li, I pass a hundred hardships without regret. One day I see my mother, and I vow to die nine deaths without a word.' Afterwards he won permission and went in to see his mother at the place of her care. She was already gravely ill, and dazed, she did not recognize her son. Zhang burned incense and appealed to Heaven, cut flesh from his thigh and made gruel, and presented it. His mother then gradually revived, and hugging her son she wept aloud. The prince, hearing of it, regarded him as a worthy, summoned him and gave him gold and silk, and commanded that he carry his mother home. Later his son, Hong, and grandson, Shan, both became Ministers of Justice, and to this day the degrees of the family have never ceased.

Liu Xunzhi, when but a child, lost both his parents. He wept and cried as if near death, and applied his heart to deep study, reciting his books often till the middle of the night. One evening his uncle heard his weeping and thought it most grievous, and asked him the reason. He said: I have been reading the Biography of Ma Zhou, and came to where he says that having lost his parents young, there was no place to offer even the support given to a dog or a horse; I am so grieved I cannot stop myself. His uncle also sighed and wept. Later he passed the examinations.

In the time of Emperor Wu of the Han, Zhang Tang and Du Zhou were both harsh officials, yet the sons of both were extremely just and forgiving. Ban Gu, in the Biographies of Harsh Officials, specially pardons Du and Zhang — for the sake of their sons. Zhang Tang's son, Anshi, served in office for thirty years, faithful and trustworthy, careful and generous, diligent in affairs; he hid men's faults and did his best to be lenient. Du Zhou's son, Yannian, assisted Huo Guang. Huo Guang applied the law severely; Yannian assisted him with leniency. Seeing the exhaustion that followed Emperor Wen's reign, he spoke to Huo Guang several times, saying one should restore the policies of the age of Emperor Wen, showing frugality and harmony, following Heaven's heart and pleasing the people's will. Huo Guang took his words. Later Anshi rose to be Grand General, and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Fuping; his descendants inherited the title one after another, and his great-grandson Chun became Grand Minister of Works. Yannian also, for his merit in settling the imperial plan, was enfeoffed as a marquis, and became Censor-in-Chief; his son Huan inherited the marquisate. The Book of Rites says: To cook cooked food and offer it fragrant, tasting it and then presenting it — this is not filial piety, but only support. What the gentleman calls filial is when the whole nation says: How happy that he has a son like this — this may be called filial. I venture to offer these as an encouragement to those who revere their parents and would cover their faults.

In the Song dynasty, Han Zhongyan was the son of Han Qi. Qi was loyal and without self, and Zhongyan, when prime minister, remitted the people's arrears, restored the exiled, and gathered and used worthy and famous men. Deng Xunwu said he was able to carry on his father's will. Again, Fan Chunren was the son of Fan Zhongyan. Zhongyan regarded the world as his own charge, and Chunren, as magistrate of Qingzhou, was arrested for righting a wrong; tens of thousands blocked his horse weeping. He passed through the Remonstrance Bureau and the Privy Council to become prime minister, and thrice was removed and thrice restored. He enlarged the lord's virtue by generosity, and did not record men's faults too deeply. When gravely ill, he still argued the slander of Empress Dowager Xuanren, and after death was honored as Loyal and Manifest (Zhongxuan). The emperor wrote the inscription on his stele: 'For generations, loyal and upright,' to show him honor. How well these two carried on the will of their sires! Set beside them those who abet evil and lack talent, disgracing their forebears — how different! Therefore the Book of Rites says: Though the parents are dead, if a man is about to do good, and thinks to leave his parents a good name, he must be resolute; if he is about to do evil and thinks to leave his parents shame, he must not do it. Again: When the parents are dead, be careful in your own conduct, and do not leave your parents an evil name — this may be called being able to carry the matter to the end. It is plain that regardless of whether the parents live or not, to be good at heart is to be filial. And for those whose parents are gone, it is precisely in this point that they can be filial. If a man harms his body and dishonors his parents, drawing the hatred and loathing of others, that is a great unfilial act.

In the Ming dynasty, Yang Shiqi was an elder statesman of four reigns, of great merit and high favor; but his son Ji, relying on his power, did evil. Shiqi doted on him and did not come to know of it. When the victim had him indicted in a dozen memorials for crimes against life, the emperor handed him to the judicial office, and by special decree consoled Shiqi, saying: Your son has departed from your family's teaching and violated the state's laws; I dare not be partial. You settle it lawfully. Shiqi, having no choice, had him sentenced to death. From this his reputation suffered greatly. Now Shiqi, as a scholar, held the state, and Ji, as a prime minister's son, was executed — ruining the family's name, putting his parents to shame, deserving blame beyond death. Those proud, noble young men who, relying on their fathers' power, act tyrannically — reading this, can they be without fear?

A wicked son of Shunyi was given a single son whom he loved beyond measure, though the child was savage by nature, regard for his mother he had none, and the mother, being old, was often beaten and cursed. One day, as she held the child, she let it slip and it fell, wounding its forehead. The wicked son returned and, thinking she had harmed his child, upbraided her in stern voice and with a terrible look. The mother, frightened, fled to her daughter's home and avoided him for several days. His anger did not subside. He hid a knife and went to greet his mother, saying: The child is recovered; come home quickly. The mother followed. On the way, at a lonely spot, he stabbed his mother in the belly. But the knife swerved and entered his own side, and his bowels spilled out — he never knew why the knife turned back. His corpse was buried again and again, and each time it rose to the surface, until the crows and wolves had eaten it clean.

Zhang Yi, every morning, confessed his faults to Heaven. Suddenly he was seized and carried into the underworld, where a black book was shown to him. The sins recorded in the book had all been blotted out, save one matter — that when young, because of a father's reproof, Zhang Yi had glared back at his father in anger. Then he knew that the sin of unfilial conduct is not to be blotted out through repentance.

Luo Gong was at the Imperial Academy, and prayed each time about his future success. One night he dreamed of a god, who said: You have already incurred guilt in the underworld; you should go home at once. Gong asked the reason. The god said: Your parents are not yet buried. Gong said: I still have an elder brother; why am I alone to suffer? The god said: You are a scholar; you know ritual and righteousness. Your elder brother is a plodding man and not to be blamed. That same year he indeed died.

When Confucius composed the Classic of Filial Piety, every evening he would fix his blue pen in his hair, put on his crimson unlined garment, face the Northern Star, and bow deeply for a long time before making his obeisance. Zengzi carried the He and Luo charts, and the seventy-two disciples all followed him — for there was a prayer. And when he composed the Spring and Autumn Annals, he did likewise. One night a black vapor suddenly came down from the Dipper and fell straight to the front of his mat. When it opened, it held a subtle meaning. This fulfilled the measure of his one heart, and set the utmost standard of human relations for ten thousand generations. The Classic of Filial Piety, in eighteen chapters, exhaustively sets forth the way of a son's serving his parents — that which is as indispensable as daily food and drink. How can the scholars of the world, because it is not listed among the subjects for the examinations, leave it untaught and unstudied? Now in discussing filial piety I return it to the Master, and trace to its source the heart with which he composed the Classic — he looked daily for scholars to practice it with their bodies, so as to aid the spread of teaching and rouse the common folk. His heart was truly good, and at the same time earnest and urgent.

inline.s: 20. Brotherly love and reverence.
21. Correct oneself to transform others.
22. Be compassionate to the orphan, pity the widow, revere the aged, cherish the young.
23. Insects, grass, and trees—even these must not be harmed.
24. One should pity others' misfortune and rejoice at others' goodness.
25. Help others in their urgency; rescue others in their peril.
26. See others' gain as one's own gain; see others' loss as one's own loss.
27. Do not expose others' failings; do not display your own strengths.
28. Suppress evil and promote good.
29. Yield the more and take the less.
30. Bear insult without resentment.
